I know that's what the docs say. Bear with me for a few hundred words and I think I can talk you out of it.

Go look at [KubeVirt](https://kubevirt.io/). It runs full virtual machines on Kubernetes. Actual VMs, the thing containers were supposed to make obsolete. So the famous container orchestrator is out here orchestrating the exact technology it was meant to replace, and nobody blinks. Or look at [Crossplane](https://www.crossplane.io/), where teams use Kubernetes to provision entire AWS accounts: S3 buckets, RDS instances, VPCs, the works. No container anywhere in the request. You write a YAML file that says "I want an RDS Postgres instance," `kubectl apply` it, and a database appears in your cloud account. The pod that eventually connects to that database is beside the point.

That's only strange if you believe Kubernetes is about containers. It isn't, and it never really was. Containers are the thing it shipped with, not the thing it is.

## What's actually in the box

Strip Kubernetes down past the workload types everyone knows and you're left with three parts:

- **A declarative API** where you record what you want, as typed, validated objects.
- **A store** that persists those objects (etcd, reached only through the API server).
- **Controllers** that watch the store, compare it to reality, and take action to close the gap.

That's the machine. Pods, Deployments, ReplicaSets, StatefulSets - these are not the essence of Kubernetes. They're the controllers that happen to come pre-installed. Someone at Google wrote a controller whose job is "make observed running pods match the desired replica count," registered a `Deployment` type for people to talk to it with, and that shipped in the box. Nothing about the underlying machinery cares that the reconciled thing is a container. Write your own controller and you can point the identical machinery at VMs, cloud accounts, Postgres databases, DNS records, TLS certificates, Cloudflare rules, whatever you can describe and drive toward a setpoint.

This is why the more honest name for Kubernetes is a **general-purpose declarative control plane**. Container orchestration is the reference architecture for that control plane - the worked example the project ships to demonstrate how a controller is supposed to behave, and the blueprint everyone copies when they build their own. Yeah, most people only ever run containers on it. That's a default, not a definition. Plenty of people only use their oven to reheat pizza.


## The control loop, and why level-triggered is the whole trick

The part worth slowing down on is what a controller actually does, because it's less clever and more durable than "it deploys your app."

A controller runs a loop. Each pass, it reads the current desired state (the `spec` of every object it watches), reads the current observed state of the real world, and if they differ, it takes one step to bring reality closer to the spec. Then it does it again. Forever. It never assumes it knows the state of the world from having caused it - it re-derives that state on every pass by looking.

This is the difference between **level-triggered** and **edge-triggered**, and it's the property that makes the whole thing hold together. An edge-triggered system reacts to events: "a Deployment was created, so create pods." Miss the event - the controller crashed, the network partitioned, a message got dropped - and the work never happens. A level-triggered controller reacts to the *current state of the world*, not to the event that produced it. Miss ten events during a crash and it doesn't matter; on restart it re-lists reality, sees the gap, and reconciles again. The event was never the source of truth. The gap between spec and reality is.

That single design choice is where drift correction, retries, and self-healing come from. You don't bolt them on. An admin changes a firewall rule in the AWS console three weeks after you deployed it? The controller's next pass sees the drift and overwrites it back to spec. A node dies and takes your pods with it? Next pass, the replica count is short, so it schedules replacements. Nobody wired up a "node died" handler. The loop just noticed the world stopped matching the request. (the mechanism, in detail)

```
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │              reconcile loop                    │
   │                                                │
   │   read desired (spec) ──┐                      │
   │                         ▼                      │
   │              ┌─────────────────┐               │
   │              │  spec == world? │──yes──▶ wait  │
   │              └────────┬────────┘               │
   │                       │ no                     │
   │                       ▼                        │
   │            take one step toward spec           │
   │                       │                        │
   │                       └───────▲ (loop again)   │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       observed world: pods, VMs, RDS, DNS, certs...
```

An imperative platform - "run these seven steps to create the database" - is only ever as correct as its last run, and it breaks the moment a step is skipped or a run dies halfway. A reconciling platform re-establishes correctness on every pass. That's the deeper reason a live control plane beats a one-shot CI pipeline, and it's worth its own [longer treatment](/blog/platform-engineering#why-a-live-api-beats-a-shift-left-check).

## CRDs: the extension point that makes it yours

If the control loop is the engine, the **CustomResourceDefinition (CRD)** is the port you plug new things into, and it's the reason "write your own controller" is a realistic sentence rather than a fork of Kubernetes.

Adding a new capability is two separable acts. First, a CRD registers a new API type. You describe the type's schema - its fields, their types, validation rules - and in return you get a full REST API for it: create, read, update, delete, watch, all with `kubectl` support, RBAC, and admission validation, for free, purely from the description. Second, a controller supplies the *behavior* that makes instances of that type do something in the world. **CRD is the type; the controller is the behavior.** A CRD with no controller behind it is just typed, validated, versioned storage - which is occasionally all you want, but usually it's the front door to a controller waiting behind it. (CRDs)

This is exactly how KubeVirt and Crossplane extend the box without modifying it. KubeVirt defines a `VirtualMachine` CRD and ships a controller that reconciles those objects against a running libvirt/QEMU process. Crossplane defines types like `RDSInstance` and ships controllers that reconcile them against the AWS API. Neither one patched Kubernetes. They registered new types and taught new controllers what those types mean. The API server didn't need to know an RDS instance from a hole in the ground - it just stored a validated object and let a controller argue with reality about it.

That CRD-plus-controller pair has a name in the ecosystem: the **operator pattern**. It's the mechanism for encoding operational knowledge that would otherwise live in a human's runbook - safe rollout order, backoff on failure, cleanup on delete, a `status` that honestly reflects reality - as a program that keeps running instead of a wiki page nobody reads at 3am. (operators)

## Why the reframe changes what you hand it

Here's the part that actually matters for how you work, and it's a shift in the question you ask.

If Kubernetes is a container orchestrator, the only sensible question is "how do I run my app on it" - how do I package my service, write the Deployment, wire the Service and Ingress, and get traffic to a pod. All real work, all container-shaped, and it caps what you get out of the system at "my processes are running."

If Kubernetes is a declarative control plane, a different question opens up: *what else can I hand it?* Anything you can describe as a typed desired state and drive toward with a control loop is a candidate to move onto the same machinery. Your S3 buckets and RDS instances become objects a controller reconciles, so a deleted bucket comes back and a changed config gets corrected - Crossplane already built that. Your TLS certificates become objects that renew themselves before expiry - cert-manager already built that. Your DNS records, your Postgres roles, your Cloudflare config, your feature-flag state, your internal "give me a preview environment" request - each becomes a CRD with a controller behind it, and each inherits the same declarative API, the same reconciliation, the same drift correction, the same RBAC and admission guardrails, the same `status` channel reporting reality back, and the same owner-reference garbage collection that makes "delete the environment" reclaim every downstream resource in order without leaking.

You stop rebuilding those properties per capability in one-off scripts and start getting them for free by expressing the capability in the control plane's native terms. That's the entire premise under Crossplane, Kratix, and the operator ecosystem: not "run more containers," but "put more of your infrastructure behind the same reconciling API." If you want to see what building on that premise looks like end to end, the [Kratix write-up](/blog/kratix) and the [hands-on platform build](/blog/building-a-platform) are the next stops.

So the practical move is small and it changes everything downstream of it. Stop asking how to run your app on Kubernetes. Start asking what else you can just hand it.
